query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A one‐step high-pressure, high-temperature (HPHT) post-treatment applied to a W–Cu composite will suppress phase separation and interfacial void formation by enhancing interfacial bonding without initiating unwanted reactions, thereby improving thermal conductivity under combined heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite containing discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix that exhibits phase segregation and void formation at the interfaces upon traditional processing and operational cycling.
generation.intervention: Subject the composite to an HPHT post-treatment process at an optimized temperature and pressure (below the melting point of Cu), designed to densify the microstructure and promote controlled interdiffusion at the W–Cu interfaces.
generation.conditions: Processing: HPHT treatment under an inert atmosphere at a temperature high enough to activate diffusion (but below the melting threshold of Cu) and pressures sufficient to suppress void nucleation; Service: Operational conditions similar to those encountered at joints between tungsten-based plasma-facing components and copper-based cooling systems under high heat flux and irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial bonding and densification due to pressure-assisted interdiffusion between W and Cu, leading to a more continuous interface with fewer voids.
generation.mechanism: High pressure reduces free volume and suppresses the nucleation and growth of voids during high-temperature processing, while elevated temperature promotes interfacial diffusion that homogenizes the interface. This dual action limits phase separation and void formation. Under service conditions, the improved interface reduces thermal barriers, maintaining high thermal conductivity despite irradiation-induced defect production.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HPHT-treated composite is expected to show a significantly reduced fraction of interfacial voids and a more homogeneous, bonded W–Cu interface, resulting in improved thermal conductivity relative to an untreated composite, even after exposure to simulated irradiation and heat-transfer cycles.
generation.baseline: The untreated W–Cu composite, which exhibits phase separation and interfacial void formation leading to lower thermal conductivity under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective if the processing parameters (temperature, pressure, duration, and atmosphere) remain within limits that prevent melting or deleterious reactions; the beneficial outcome is expected under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions representative of plasma-facing joint environments in fusion reactors.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal HPHT parameters (exact temperature, pressure, and treatment time) and the long-term stability of the modified interface under prolonged irradiation conditions remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical W–Cu composite samples; apply the HPHT post-treatment to one set while keeping the other set as untreated controls. Then subject both sets to simulated service conditions involving representative heat-transfer cycles and irradiation. Use cross-sectional microscopy (TEM/SEM) to examine the W–Cu interfaces for void formation and phase separation, and measure thermal conductivity and interfacial resistance before and after the treatment and service simulation.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of interfacial void fraction using high-resolution TEM/SEM.
Thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., via laser flash analysis).
Elemental diffusion profiles across the interface (e.g., via EDS or SIMS).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HPHT-treated composite does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in interfacial void fraction accompanied by improved thermal conductivity (relative to the untreated samples) after simulated operational conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Clean energy production is the cornerstone of our time. Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering
